ety.text: From истреби́ть (istrebítʹ) + -тель (-telʹ). The nautical sense, attested early 20th century, was a semantic loan from English destroyer; the aviation sense, attested in the 1910s and by far the predominant one in modern usage, evolved from the nautical sense.
A Turkic borrowing: compare Uyghur قاتتىق (qattiq, “hard”).
Derived from Ancient Greek κάθετος (káthetos) (via Latin cathetus). Compare natively formed Czech odvěsna (i.e. отве́сная (otvésnaja)), Polish przyprostokątna (i.e. **припростоку́тная).

ety.text: Per Vasmer, perhaps a modification of огороди́ть (ogorodítʹ, “to fence in”), influenced by лапо́шить (lapóšitʹ, “to bother”), копоши́ться (kopošítʹsja, “to swarm”). Per Shansky and Krylov from горо́шить (goróšitʹ), from горо́х (goróx). Compare как об сте́нку горо́х (kak ob sténku goróx), сы́пать как горо́х (sýpatʹ kak goróx). Also compare оста́ться на боба́х (ostátʹsja na bobáx) (< боб (bob)), на оре́хи (na oréxi) (< оре́х (oréx)). In addition, the relation with Ukrainian горохнуть (horoxnutʹ), and further with гро́хнуть (gróxnutʹ), гро́хать (gróxatʹ) was supposed by Anikin.

s.g: to spread quickly (e.g. of a fire)
